lessons.title: A Christmas Carol: characters
lessons.summary: Explore how Dickens presents Scrooge, the Cratchits, Fred, Marley, the three Spirits and the minor characters, and how each one serves the novella's moral purpose.
objectives: I can track Scrooge's transformation using quotations from each stave.
I can explain the roles of Bob Cratchit, Tiny Tim, Fred, Marley and Fezziwig as contrasts or warnings.
I can describe how each of the three Spirits looks and behaves, and what each represents.
I can explain what Belle, Fan, Mrs Cratchit and the allegorical children Ignorance and Want contribute.
I can write an analytical paragraph about a character that links method to Dickens's purpose.

activities.title: Scrooge before the Spirits
activities.content:
## Scrooge in Stave One

Dickens builds Scrooge through **exaggeration** (a technique called **caricature**), so that his change will be as dramatic as possible.

**Cold.** He is *"Hard and sharp as flint"* and *"solitary as an oyster"*. The cold inside him *"froze his old features"* and he carries *"his own low temperature"* everywhere. No weather can touch him because he is already colder than it is.

**Mean.** He keeps his clerk's fire to *"one coal"*, keeps his own rooms dark because *"darkness is cheap"*, and eats gruel alone.

**Isolated by choice.** Nobody stops him in the street to say hello, and *"what did Scrooge care? It was the very thing he liked."*

**Politically hard.** His replies to the charity collectors are the language of the 1834 Poor Law: prisons, workhouses, the treadmill. He calls the poor *"surplus population"*, echoing the economist Malthus.

**But not without wit.** His *"Bah! Humbug!"* and his joke that Marley's ghost is a bit of undigested beef show a lively mind. Dickens gives him energy so that the reader can imagine that energy turned to good.

**Key idea:** Scrooge is not born evil. The list of adjectives (*"squeezing, wrenching, grasping..."*) describes a man who has become a machine for taking; the Spirits will show us how.

activities.title: Tracking Scrooge across the staves
activities.content:
Use a **character timeline** with one quotation per stave.

| Stave | Quotation | What it shows |
|---|---|---|
| One | *"solitary as an oyster"* | Closed, hard shell; but an oyster may hide a pearl |
| Two | *"I should like to have given him something"* (of the carol-singer) | First regret, prompted by his own lonely childhood |
| Three | *"Tell me if Tiny Tim will live"* | Concern for someone else, for the first time |
| Four | *"I am not the man I was"* | He claims the change before the Spirit confirms it |
| Five | *"I am as light as a feather, I am as happy as an angel"* | Similes of weightlessness replace the frost imagery |

**Model sentence:** *"Dickens tracks Scrooge's transformation through his changing similes: the 'oyster' of Stave One, hard and shut, becomes the 'feather' of Stave Five, so light that nothing weighs him down. The shift from cold, heavy images to warm, weightless ones lets the reader feel the change rather than merely be told about it."*

**Why it works:** it shows development, it names the method (simile, imagery), and it explains the effect on the reader.

question.text: Put these moments in Scrooge's transformation in the order they happen.
question.hint: Move from the cold opening through regret, concern and pleading to joy.
question.explanation: Stave One: 'solitary as an oyster'. Stave Two: regret over the carol-singer. Stave Three: asking whether Tiny Tim will live. Stave Four: begging at the gravestone. Stave Five: 'as light as a feather'.
order: Scrooge is described as 'solitary as an oyster'
Scrooge wishes he had given the carol-singer something
Scrooge asks whether Tiny Tim will live
Scrooge begs the Spirit for a chance to change at the gravestone
Scrooge declares he is 'as light as a feather'

activities.title: The Cratchits and Tiny Tim
activities.content:
## The Cratchit family

**Bob Cratchit** is Scrooge's clerk, paid fifteen shillings a week. Dickens presents him as everything Scrooge is not: warm, playful (he slides on the ice on Christmas Eve), forgiving. At the family dinner he toasts Scrooge as *"the Founder of the Feast"*, even though Scrooge founded very little. His grief in Stave Four, when he says *"My little, little child!"*, is the emotional centre of the book.

**Mrs Cratchit** is loyal but not meek. She calls Scrooge *"an odious, stingy, hard, unfeeling man"* and only toasts him for Bob's sake. Through her, Dickens lets the reader hear an honest verdict.

**Tiny Tim** is small, lame and good. He hopes people will see him in church and remember *"who made lame beggars walk, and blind men see."* His *"God bless us every one!"* frames the book. Dickens uses him as a **symbol** of the innocent poor: Scrooge's attitude to Tim is the test of his heart. The Spirit's prediction of an *"empty chair"* makes the abstract idea of poverty deadly and personal.

**Why the Cratchits matter**

- They show that **happiness does not depend on money**: their tiny pudding is treated as a triumph.
- They give the reader a **family to care about**, so that political ideas become feelings.
- They are the **measure of Scrooge's change**: the turkey and the pay rise go to them.

question.text: How does Dickens use Tiny Tim to influence the reader's feelings about poverty? Refer to at least one detail from the text.
question.hint: Consider his goodness, the prediction about the empty chair, and how Scrooge reacts.
question.explanation: Tim is presented as innocent and good, hoping people will remember Christ's healing of the lame, so the reader cannot blame him for his poverty. The Spirit's vision of the 'empty chair' and Bob's grief in Stave Four make the consequence of poverty a child's death rather than a statistic. Scrooge's concern for Tim becomes the test of his change, so the reader is led to share that concern.

markScheme.criterion: AO1: Describes Tim as innocent, good or symbolic of the deserving poor with a textual detail (church, 'God bless us', crutch, empty chair)
AO2: Explains the emotional effect (sympathy, pity, making poverty personal or a real child rather than a statistic)
AO3: Links to Dickens's purpose or Victorian attitudes to the poor (Poor Law, Malthus, surplus population, social reform)

activities.title: Fred, Marley and Fezziwig: three mirrors
activities.content:
## Characters who reflect Scrooge

Dickens surrounds Scrooge with characters who show what he **could be** or what he **will become**.

**Fred** (his nephew) is the opposite of Scrooge in the same family. He is *"all in a glow"* when he enters, has little money and a wife Scrooge disapproves of, yet insists Christmas is *"a good time; a kind, forgiving, charitable, pleasant time."* He refuses to give up on his uncle, laughing at him but pitying him. Fred is the voice of Dickens's Christmas philosophy, and he is also Fan's son, a living link to the sister Scrooge loved.

**Jacob Marley** is Scrooge's future if nothing changes. His chain of *"cash-boxes, keys, padlocks, ledgers"* is the physical form of a life spent on money. His cry that *"Mankind was my business"* rejects Scrooge's idea that business is only about profit. Marley's torment is that he now wants to help but cannot: the phantoms outside the window all share this punishment.

**Fezziwig** is the model employer. His Christmas party costs *"a few pounds"* but fills the room with joy. Watching, Scrooge realises that the power to make employees happy *"is quite as great as if it cost a fortune."* He immediately thinks of Bob Cratchit: Fezziwig is the template for the boss Scrooge becomes in Stave Five.

**Exam tip:** describe these characters as **foils** (contrasts that highlight Scrooge's qualities) and explain what Dickens uses each to argue.

activities.title: Writing about a foil
activities.content:
**Question:** How does Dickens use Fred to present ideas about Christmas?

**Model paragraph**

Dickens uses Fred as a **foil** to Scrooge: everything the uncle rejects, the nephew embraces. Fred defends Christmas as *"the only time I know of... when men and women seem by one consent to open their shut-up hearts freely."* The metaphor of *"shut-up hearts"* echoes the earlier description of Scrooge as *"solitary as an oyster"*, so that Fred's speech becomes a diagnosis of his uncle without naming him. The verb *"open"* is what the whole novella asks Scrooge to do. Because Fred says this in Stave One, before the Spirits arrive, Dickens establishes that the cure for Scrooge is already available in ordinary human kindness; the supernatural only forces him to accept it. For a Victorian reader, Fred models the warm, family-centred Christmas that Dickens was helping to popularise.

**Notice**

- The paragraph names the character's **function** (foil).
- It connects Fred's language to Scrooge's imagery.
- It uses **structure** (when Fred speaks) to make a point.
- Context arrives at the end and links to purpose.

question.text: Match each character to the role they play in the novella.
question.hint: Think about what each character shows Scrooge or the reader.
question.explanation: Marley is a warning of Scrooge's future; Fezziwig is the model of a generous employer; Fred is the voice of Christmas spirit and family; Belle shows what Scrooge lost to his love of money.

pairs.right: A warning of what Scrooge will become if he does not change
A model of the generous employer Scrooge could be
The voice of the Christmas spirit and family warmth
The love Scrooge lost to his 'golden idol'

activities.title: The three Spirits
activities.content:
## The Spirits as characters and symbols

**The Ghost of Christmas Past** is a contradiction: *"like a child: yet not so like a child as like an old man"*, with a jet of bright light springing from its head. Memory is like this: fresh as a child, ancient as an old man, and illuminating. Its cap can put out the light, and Scrooge uses it to end the visions, showing his wish to suppress painful memory. Its manner is gentle but firm.

**The Ghost of Christmas Present** is a *"jolly Giant"* in a green robe on a throne of food, with a torch that sprinkles blessing. It represents **generosity and abundance**, but it also carries the sharpest social criticism: it repeats Scrooge's words back to him and reveals **Ignorance and Want** under its robe. It lives only one day and ages visibly, showing that the chance to act is short.

**The Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come** is a *"Phantom"* that *"neither spoke nor moved"*, shrouded in black, with only a pointing hand visible. Its silence forces Scrooge to interpret and to speak for himself, which is how Dickens shows that the change now comes from within. It resembles the Grim Reaper, so it embodies death.

**Ignorance and Want** are *"wretched, abject, frightful, hideous, miserable"* children, personifications of society's neglect. The Spirit warns *"most of all beware this boy"*: ignorance, left untreated, leads to *"Doom"*. Dickens believed education was the cure for poverty.

question.text: Why is it significant that the Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come never speaks?
question.hint: Who has to do the talking and interpreting in Stave Four?
question.explanation: Because the Spirit is silent, Scrooge must interpret the visions and voice his own conclusions. This shows that the change now comes from inside him, not from being lectured.

options.text: Scrooge must interpret the visions himself, showing the change now comes from within
It cannot speak because it is not really a ghost
Dickens wanted to save space in the final stave
It has already told Scrooge everything in Stave One

question.text: Complete the sentences about minor characters.

metadata.blanksText: Scrooge's younger sister, ___, comes to bring him home from school and later dies leaving one child. Bob Cratchit's wife calls Scrooge an "odious, stingy, hard, unfeeling ___". The two children hidden under the robe of the Ghost of Christmas Present are called Ignorance and ___.

question.hint: A short name beginning with F; a noun for a person; the partner of Ignorance.
question.explanation: Fan is the loving sister; Mrs Cratchit's honest verdict is 'man'; the allegorical children are Ignorance and Want.

question.text: True or false: Mrs Cratchit shares her husband's forgiving attitude and gladly drinks to Scrooge's health.
question.hint: Read her reaction to Bob's toast at the Christmas dinner.
question.explanation: False. Mrs Cratchit objects strongly, calling Scrooge odious and stingy, and drinks only for Bob's sake and because it is Christmas. Dickens uses her to voice a blunt, honest judgement.

question.text:
Starting with this extract from Stave One, explore how Dickens presents Scrooge as an outsider to society.

*"Nobody ever stopped him in the street to say, with gladsome looks, 'My dear Scrooge, how are you?' No beggars implored him to bestow a trifle, no children asked him what it was o'clock... But what did Scrooge care! It was the very thing he liked."*

Write two or three developed paragraphs. Analyse the language in the extract, refer to Scrooge elsewhere in the novella, and link your ideas to Dickens's purpose.
question.hint: Plan: (1) the list of things that do not happen and the repetition of 'no', (2) Scrooge's choice of isolation ('the very thing he liked') and the oyster simile, (3) how isolation is shown as its own punishment through Marley and the vision of his unmourned death, (4) how Stave Five reverses this as Scrooge walks the streets greeting people.
question.explanation: A strong answer notes the accumulation of negatives ('Nobody', 'No beggars', 'no children'), which defines Scrooge by absence: even the poorest avoid him. The exclamation 'what did Scrooge care!' and the narrator's ironic voice show isolation is chosen, echoing 'solitary as an oyster'. Elsewhere Dickens shows this choice punished: Marley's chain, the unmourned corpse in Stave Four, the businessmen joking about his funeral. Stave Five reverses the extract: Scrooge walks the streets, greets people and rejoins society. Dickens's purpose was to argue, against Victorian individualism, that 'mankind' is everyone's business.

markScheme.criterion: AO1: Makes a clear point that Scrooge is isolated or an outsider, and that he chooses it
AO2: Analyses the repeated negatives or list ('Nobody', 'No beggars', 'no children')
AO2: Analyses the narrator's ironic tone or the exclamation 'what did Scrooge care!'
AO1: Refers to another image of isolation elsewhere (oyster, flint, cold, darkness is cheap)
AO1: Refers to the consequences of isolation (Marley, the unmourned death, businessmen, Old Joe's)
AO2: Comments on the reversal in Stave Five (walking the streets, greeting people, rejoining society)
AO3: Links to Dickens's purpose or Victorian context (individualism, 'mankind was my business', social responsibility)
AO2: Uses subject terminology accurately (simile, hyperbole, caricature, narrator, symbol)

activities.title: Key points
activities.content:
- **Scrooge**: caricature of coldness ('oyster', 'flint') who becomes 'light as a feather'. Track him stave by stave.
- **The Cratchits**: warmth without wealth; Bob forgives, Mrs Cratchit judges, Tiny Tim symbolises the innocent poor and tests Scrooge's heart.
- **Fred**: foil and voice of Christmas; refuses to give up on his uncle.
- **Marley**: Scrooge's future; 'Mankind was my business'.
- **Fezziwig**: the model employer; happiness costs 'a few pounds'.
- **Belle and Fan**: the love Scrooge lost and the sister who shaped him.
- **The Spirits**: Past (memory, light), Present (abundance and social criticism), Yet to Come (silent death).
- **Ignorance and Want**: allegory of society's neglect; 'beware this boy'.
- Write about **function**: what does Dickens use each character to argue?

practiceQuestions.text: Which simile does Dickens use to describe Scrooge's isolation in Stave One?
practiceQuestions.hint: It compares him to a sea creature with a hard shell.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Scrooge is 'solitary as an oyster': closed, hard and alone, though an oyster may hide a pearl.

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: Fred is the son of Scrooge's sister Fan.
practiceQuestions.hint: The Ghost of Christmas Past reminds Scrooge that Fan had one child.
practiceQuestions.explanation: True. Fan died leaving one child, Fred. Scrooge's rejection of Fred is also a rejection of Fan's memory.

practiceQuestions.text: Match each quotation to the character who says it.
practiceQuestions.hint: One is about business, one is a blessing, one is about an idol.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Marley insists 'Mankind was my business'; Tiny Tim says 'God bless us every one!'; Belle tells Scrooge that a 'golden idol' has replaced her.

pairs.left: "Another idol has displaced me... a golden one"

metadata.blanksText: Bob Cratchit toasts Scrooge as "the Founder of the ___", and in Stave Five Scrooge becomes "a second ___" to Tiny Tim.

practiceQuestions.hint: A word for a celebration meal; a family role.
practiceQuestions.explanation: 'Founder of the Feast' is Bob's generous (and ironic) toast; Scrooge becomes 'a second father' to Tim.

practiceQuestions.text: What does the Ghost of Christmas Past's extinguisher-cap most clearly represent?
practiceQuestions.hint: Scrooge uses it to end the visions he cannot bear.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The cap can put out the light of memory. When Scrooge presses it down, he is trying to suppress painful memories, though the light still streams out beneath it.

options.text: Scrooge's wish to suppress painful memories

practiceQuestions.text: Explain how Dickens uses Marley's Ghost to warn both Scrooge and the reader. Refer to the chain and to Marley's words.
practiceQuestions.hint: What is the chain made of, who made it, and what does Marley say about 'business'?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Marley's chain is made of cash-boxes, ledgers and padlocks, forged 'link by link' in life, so it is a physical symbol of a money-obsessed existence. Marley says Scrooge's own chain was already as long seven years ago, warning that he is building his own punishment. His cry that 'Mankind was my business' redefines business as social responsibility, a message aimed at Dickens's readers as much as at Scrooge.

markScheme.criterion: AO1/AO2: Describes the chain as a symbol of a life devoted to money (cash-boxes, ledgers, forged in life)
AO1: Explains that Scrooge is building his own chain / will suffer the same fate
AO3: Explains 'Mankind was my business' as a message about social responsibility aimed at readers

practiceQuestions.text: Which of the following are ways Dickens creates sympathy for Scrooge in Stave Two? Select **all** that apply.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about what the Ghost of Christmas Past reveals about his childhood and youth.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Showing the neglected schoolboy and the loss of Belle explains how Scrooge became hard, creating sympathy. Marley's chain is a warning, not sympathy, and Mrs Cratchit's verdict is criticism.

options.text: Showing him as a lonely boy left at school over Christmas
Showing Belle leaving him and the happy family life he lost
Mrs Cratchit calling him odious and stingy

practiceQuestions.text: Put the following characters in the order Scrooge meets or sees them in the novella.
practiceQuestions.hint: Start in the counting-house and end with the silent phantom.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Fred visits the counting-house in Stave One, Marley appears that night, Fezziwig is seen in Stave Two, the Ghost of Christmas Present shows Tiny Tim in Stave Three, and the silent phantom comes in Stave Four.
order: The Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come

practiceQuestions.text:
How does Dickens present the Cratchit family as a contrast to Scrooge?

Write two developed paragraphs. Use quotations or close references, analyse Dickens's methods, and link your ideas to Victorian attitudes to poverty.
practiceQuestions.hint: Consider warmth versus cold, the small feast treated as abundance, Bob's forgiveness, Mrs Cratchit's honesty, and how the family is the measure of Scrooge's change.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The Cratchits are poor but rich in warmth: their goose and tiny pudding are celebrated as if they were a feast, contrasting with Scrooge's gruel eaten alone. Bob's forgiving toast contrasts with Scrooge's contempt, while Mrs Cratchit's blunt verdict voices what the reader thinks. Dickens uses warmth and light imagery for their home against the cold and dark of Scrooge's. The family also measures Scrooge's change, since his generosity flows to them. Dickens challenges the Victorian idea that the poor deserved their poverty by presenting a hard-working, loving family that only lacks money.

markScheme.criterion: AO1: Contrasts the Cratchits' warmth or happiness with Scrooge's coldness or isolation
AO1: Uses a specific reference (goose, pudding, 'Founder of the Feast', Tiny Tim, fifteen shillings)
AO2: Analyses a method (imagery of warmth and light, hyperbole about the feast, contrast, symbolism)
AO1: Discusses Bob's forgiveness or Mrs Cratchit's honest judgement
AO2: Explains the Cratchits as the measure of Scrooge's change (turkey, pay rise, second father)
AO3: Links to Victorian attitudes to the poor (deserving/undeserving, Poor Law, workhouses, Dickens's own childhood)

practiceQuestions.text: What do the children Ignorance and Want represent, and why does the Spirit say Scrooge should beware the boy most of all?
practiceQuestions.hint: They are personifications of social problems. What did Dickens think was the root cause of poverty?
practiceQuestions.explanation: They personify the ignorance and poverty that society creates by neglecting the poor. The Spirit warns most against Ignorance because, if left untreated, lack of education leads to 'Doom' for society; Dickens believed education was the key to ending poverty.

markScheme.criterion: Explains them as personifications or symbols of society's neglect, poverty and lack of education
Explains that ignorance is the root cause or leads to 'Doom' / that education is the cure

practiceQuestions.text: Put these moments involving Bob Cratchit in the order they happen in the novella.
practiceQuestions.hint: Bob's toast comes in the present-day vision; his grief is in the future vision.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Bob warms himself at a candle in Stave One, then slides down Cornhill on his way home the same evening. He toasts Scrooge at the Christmas dinner in Stave Three, is shown grieving for Tiny Tim in Stave Four, and receives a pay rise in Stave Five.
order: Bob tries to warm himself at a candle in Scrooge's counting-house
Bob slides down Cornhill with the boys on his way home
Bob toasts Scrooge as the Founder of the Feast
Bob breaks down after visiting Tiny Tim's grave in the vision of the future
Scrooge tells Bob he is going to raise his salary

practiceQuestions.text: How does Dickens use Fred to influence the reader's view of Christmas and of Scrooge? Refer to at least one detail from the text.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about how Fred behaves in the counting-house, what he says Christmas is, and how he talks about his uncle at the party.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Fred arrives glowing with cold and good humour, invites his uncle to dinner despite being insulted, and defends Christmas as a kind, forgiving, charitable time; at his party he pities Scrooge rather than mocking him. As a foil, his warmth makes Scrooge's coldness look unnatural and shows the reader that the Christmas spirit is generous and persistent. Dickens uses him to promote the family Christmas of goodwill that the novella celebrates and to show that Scrooge is never beyond reach.

markScheme.criterion: AO1: Describes Fred as cheerful, warm, kind or forgiving with a textual detail (the invitation, defending Christmas, pitying Scrooge)
AO2: Explains his effect as a foil or contrast that makes Scrooge look cold or unnatural and puts the reader on Christmas's side
AO3: Links to Dickens's purpose or Victorian ideas of a family Christmas and goodwill

practiceQuestions.text: Match each minor character to their role in the novella.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about who belongs to Scrooge's past, who tests his generosity, who profits from his death, and who shares his youth.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Fan is Scrooge's loving sister who brings him home from school. The charity collectors give Scrooge a chance to be generous, which he refuses. Old Joe buys the goods stolen from the dead man's room. Dick Wilkins is Scrooge's fellow apprentice at Fezziwig's.

pairs.right: Scrooge's loving sister who fetches him home from school
Offer Scrooge a chance to give to the poor, which he refuses
Buys the belongings stolen from the dead man's room
Scrooge's fellow apprentice at Fezziwig's warehouse

practiceQuestions.text: Why does Dickens give the Ghost of Christmas Present an empty scabbard with no sword in it?
practiceQuestions.hint: A scabbard is for carrying a weapon. What does it suggest if the weapon has been removed and the scabbard is rusty?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The empty, rusty scabbard symbolises peace and goodwill: the Spirit of Christmas has no use for violence. This fits its generous, abundant character.

options.text: To symbolise peace and goodwill, showing that Christmas has no use for violence
To show that the Spirit has lost a battle
options.feedback: The scabbard is a symbol, not a sign of defeat.

options.text: To suggest that Scrooge has stolen the sword
To show that the Spirit is powerless
options.feedback: The Spirit is powerful; it simply does not use force.

practiceQuestions.text: Complete the sentences about the Cratchit family.

metadata.blanksText: Scrooge's underpaid clerk is called ___ Cratchit. His eldest daughter, ___, works long hours at a milliner's. His son ___ hopes to get a job paying five shillings and sixpence a week.

practiceQuestions.hint: The clerk's first name is short; the daughter arrives late for dinner; the son wears his father's shirt collar.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Bob Cratchit is the clerk. Martha works at a milliner's and arrives late on Christmas Day. Peter is offered a job at five and sixpence a week.

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: Belle ends her engagement to Scrooge because she has fallen in love with another man.
practiceQuestions.hint: What does Belle say has taken her place in Scrooge's heart?
practiceQuestions.explanation: False. Belle releases Scrooge because a 'golden idol', his love of money, has replaced her. She marries someone else only years later.

options.feedback: She leaves because money has become his idol, not because of another man.

practiceQuestions.text:
Starting with this moment from Stave Two, explore how Dickens presents Fezziwig and the effect he has on Scrooge.

*After the party, the Ghost of Christmas Past remarks that Fezziwig has spent only a few pounds of "mortal money" and asks whether he really deserves such praise. Scrooge, speaking like his younger self, replies that the happiness Fezziwig gives is as great "as if it cost a fortune". He then falls quiet and says he would like to say a word or two to his own clerk.*

Write two or three developed paragraphs. Analyse the language in this moment, refer to Fezziwig and to Scrooge's treatment of Bob elsewhere in the novella, and link your ideas to Dickens's purpose.
practiceQuestions.hint: Explain the Spirit's ironic question about money and Scrooge's answer about happiness. Contrast Fezziwig's party with the way Scrooge treats Bob in Stave One, and think about how this memory pays off in Stave Five.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A strong answer presents Fezziwig as the model of a generous employer and a foil to Scrooge. The Spirit's question about 'mortal money' is ironic, echoing Scrooge's own values, and Scrooge's reply that happiness is worth as much as a fortune shows him briefly recovering the values of his youth. His wish to speak to his clerk is the first sign of change. The party itself, with its fiddler, dancing and warehouse made snug and warm, contrasts with Stave One, where Scrooge denies Bob coal and complains that a day's holiday is like picking his pocket. Structurally the memory pays off in Stave Five when Scrooge raises Bob's salary over a bowl of smoking bishop. Dickens's purpose is to show Victorian employers that kindness costs little and that responsibility for workers is part of the Christmas spirit.

markScheme.criterion: AO1: Makes a clear point that Fezziwig is a generous, ideal employer and a contrast to Scrooge
AO2: Analyses the Spirit's ironic question about 'mortal money' or Scrooge's reply weighing happiness against cost
AO2: Comments on Scrooge speaking like his former self or his wish to speak to his clerk as the first sign of change
AO1: Refers to details of the party elsewhere (fiddler, dancing, the warehouse transformed, Mrs Fezziwig)
AO1: Contrasts with Scrooge's treatment of Bob in Stave One (coal, the fire, the holiday as picking his pocket, fifteen shillings)
AO2: Comments on the structural role of the memory and its payoff in Stave Five (the raise, smoking bishop)
AO3: Links to Victorian context or Dickens's purpose (employers' responsibility, working conditions)
AO2: Uses subject terminology accurately (foil, caricature, symbol, narrator, imagery)
